answer: According to the corpus (Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's 100 metres, doc Q116495917), the 2024 men's 100m final was one of the most tightly contested in history because: (1) the final contained 6 men with top-25 all-time 100m records, and the gap between the fastest man in the field (Fred Kerley, 9.76) and the slowest (Kenny Bednarek, 9.87) was only 0.11 seconds; (2) for the first time in 100m history, all 8 finalists had run under 10 seconds in the semi-finals (12 of 27 semi-finalists went sub-10, with just 0.05 seconds between 8th-placed Bednarek and 12th-placed Andre De Grasse); (3) the gap between 1st and 8th place was only 0.12 seconds — the closest and fastest 100m race in history, and the first time the entire field broke 10 seconds in a competitive race, with places 5–8 running the fastest times in history for those positions; and (4) Noah Lyles won in 9.784, just 0.005 seconds ahead of Kishane Thompson's 9.789 (both officially 9.79), described as possibly the closest 1–2 finish in Olympic 100m history, with Fred Kerley taking bronze in 9.81, just 0.01 ahead of Akani Simbine (9.82, a South African national record).
explanation: The answer is drawn entirely from the event article Q116495917, which explicitly states the final was "one of the most tightly contested in history" and lists the supporting facts: 6 top-25 all-time performers, 0.11-second spread between fastest and slowest entrants, all 8 finalists sub-10 in semis (a first), 0.12-second 1st-to-8th gap (closest/fastest ever, first full sub-10 field), and Lyles' 0.005-second win over Thompson (9.784 vs 9.789).
